To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
social class differences in academic engagement are rooted in differences in the strategies undergraduates use to succeed in college.

(1) First-generation and middle class undergraduates expend strenuous efforts in their first two years at an urban, comprehensive university; (2) First-generation students employ independent strategies to succeed in college, while middle class students employ interactive, as well independent, strategies; and (3) Middle class students’ broader repertoire of strategies includes those that are visible, recognized, and rewarded by faculty and staff at the university, while first-generation students’ independent strategies are largely invisible and ignored.
first generation and middle class undergraduates have different strategies of engagement, which are shaped by their social class background.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how students’ strategies of engagement are shaped by the institutional context and how these differences contribute to the reproduction of social class inequality in higher education.

the ways in which the academic experiences of first-generation and middle-class students are shaped and constrained by the social and cultural resources they bring to college and the ways they are recognized and rewarded by the college environment.
the social class differences in undergraduates’ academic engagement strategies and their implications for educational inequality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the social class differences in undergraduates’ academic engagement strategies are a function of the institutional rules and the students’ cultural resources.

social class differences in academic strategies reflect social class differences in students’ cultural capital, which is shaped in part by the rules of engagement that are implicit in the college context and are reinforced by faculty and staff.
social class shapes undergrads’ academic strategies, which are rewarded by the college context, and that these rewards are unequally distributed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
social class differences in undergraduates’ academic engagement are not simply the product of students’ backgrounds, but also reflect the rules of engagement in the university.
the social class of undergraduates shapes their academic engagement strategies, which are in turn rewarded or not by the university.
the middle class is more likely to be rewarded by the system because they are more likely to be seen as fitting into the system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
institutions need to recognize the value of independent strategies and to make them more visible in order to reduce the social class gap in academic outcomes.
institutions need to recognize and reward all students’ strategies for success.
the college field is not a level playing field.
